steps.say: A circuit needs a complete loop with no gaps. A switch opens and closes a gap in the loop.
Scientists draw circuits with symbols. A cell is a long and a short line, and a bulb is a circle with a cross.

figure.alt: A circuit diagram with a battery, a lit bulb and a closed switch in one loop.

steps.say: Adding more cells gives a bigger push, so bulbs get brighter. Too many cells can make a bulb burn out.
Adding more bulbs in the same loop makes each bulb dimmer. They share the push from the cells.
Conductors, such as metals, let electricity flow. Insulators, such as plastic and rubber, do not.
In 1800, Alessandro Volta made the first battery from zinc and copper discs with salty cardboard between them.
Never play with electricity from wall sockets. It is much more powerful than cells and is dangerous.

check.prompt: What does a switch do in a circuit?

options.why: A switch does not change the cells.

options.text: changes the colour of the bulb
options.why: A switch only turns the circuit on or off.

options.text: opens or closes a gap in the circuit

options.why: Cells store energy. A switch just opens or closes the loop.

hints: Electricity flows only around a complete loop.
Think about what happens when you flick a light switch off.
Cross out the choices about colour and storing.
check.explanation: A switch opens or closes a gap in the circuit. When it is closed, the loop is complete and electricity flows.

check.prompt: A circuit has 2 cells and 1 bulb. One cell is taken out and the wires are joined again. What happens to the bulb?

options.why: Fewer cells give a smaller push, so the bulb does not get brighter.
The push from the cells changes, so the brightness changes.
The bulb stays on, just less brightly.

hints: Cells push electricity around the circuit.
Fewer cells give a smaller push.
Think about what a smaller push does to a bulb.
check.explanation: With only one cell, the push is smaller, so less electricity flows and the bulb is dimmer.
